title: Hub had meetings at the European Parliament to advocate for a dedicated place and funding for culture and cultural heritage in future Horizon Europe and European Competitiveness Fund
content: As negotiations on the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) — the EU’s next long-term budget for 2028-2034 — continue, Europa Nostra, in its capacity as Project Leader of the European Heritage Hub, and representing the European Heritage Hub Consortium and the European Heritage Alliance, is stepping up the call for culture and cultural heritage to have a clearly recognised and adequately funded place in the EU’s future research, innovation and competitiveness programmes.

title: Culture as Democratic Infrastructure in a Changing Europe
content:
In Varietate Concordia — United in Diversity — captures one of Europe’s most enduring ambitions. Yet today, this principle is under increasing strain. Across the continent and beyond, societies are facing rising polarisation, declining trust in institutions, widening inequalities, rapid digital transformation, and the accelerating impacts of climate change. These pressures are not only political or economic — they are fundamentally relational. They shape how people perceive one another, how they interact, and how they imagine shared futures.

In this context, culture and heritage are often positioned as supportive or secondary policy domains. However, growing evidence suggests a different interpretation: culture and heritage function as critical democratic infrastructure. They shape the conditions under which democratic values are practiced, negotiated and sustained in everyday life (European Commission, 2023; Council of Europe, 2010). This article argues that culture should not be understood simply as a sector, but as an ecosystem of relationships and practices through which societies organise meaning, trust, identity and collective action.

title: The Living Past: Experimental Archaeology and Reenactment as a Shared Language for a Democratic Future
content:
Culture is a living process that belongs to everyone. Through more than twenty years of international experience in this field, I’ve seen how moving history out of textbooks and into the hands of the public can be a gamechanger. Living history and experimental archaeology go far beyond “reconstruction”: they are powerful, democratic tools that foster critical thinking and social cohesion. When you see a researcher sweating over a primitive forge or a weaver explaining an ancient technique, you’re looking at a shared language that everyone can understand, regardless of their background or education. It makes heritage inclusive in a way that academic lectures often can’t.

However, the quality of this “language” depends on the strength of our professional networks. A great example of this is the international Association of Experimental Archaeology, Open-Air Museums, Traditional Crafts, and Heritage Interpretation (EXARC). In its 25 years of work, it has shown how vital it is to connect open-air museums, universities, and practitioners. This kind of synergy is what keeps the field scientifically grounded.

title: What I Feel When I Think of Europe: Beyond Treaties, Through Heritage
content:
From as long as I can remember, I have felt Europe remarkably close: in its cities, in its landscapes, and in the people who turn it into an interwoven fabric of brotherly nations. This closeness has led me to understand that what truly sustains a society is not only treaties or institutions, but the bonds that unite its citizens.

From my perspective, a fair and democratic society depends on well-being, shared values, and the cohesion of its population. For this reason, the preservation of cultural heritage, both tangible and intangible, becomes an essential pillar for building more committed, critical, and transformative societies.

Cultural heritage is a living tool that helps us remember who we are, through its multiple forms of heritage (architectural, folkloric, gastronomic). Through it, we find shared values and points of connection that transcend social and generational differences. In today’s European context, marked by diversity and polarisation, this ability to generate belonging is key to strengthening social cohesion.

title: Join the Hub’s high-level online Policy Talk on how cultural heritage should fit into future European AI policies
content:
What if Europe could shape an approach to AI that puts the public interest first? And what role can cultural heritage play?

To answer these questions and more, join the European Heritage Hub for the high-level online Policy Talk “INNOVATE. PROTECT. EMPOWER.: How cultural heritage can make Public AI a reality,” on 29 September at 16:00-18:00 CET.

This high-level event is organised by Europeana within the framework and support of the European Heritage Hub EU-funded Preparatory Action. It will bring together European and international policymakers, innovators and leaders from across the cultural heritage and AI communities, aiming to catalyse a coordinated advocacy movement around shared policy priorities and a common vision for Public AI.  

AI is rapidly transforming our societies, economies and cultural sectors. At the same time, a new vision is emerging: Public AI — a more democratic, pluralistic and publicly accountable approach to AI, grounded in the public interest.

title: How Rotterdam is reinventing religious heritage for city life
content:
Rotterdam has spent much of its modern history reinventing itself. Rebuilt after the devastation of the Second World War, the city became a testing ground for new ideas in architecture, planning and urban development. The spirit of reconstruction remains deeply embedded in Rotterdam’s identity, shaping a city where innovation and adaptation are part of everyday life.

This legacy has also shaped Rotterdam’s relationship with its own past. With much of its historic urban fabric destroyed in 1940, the city cannot draw on an extensive stock of pre-war monuments to sustain a sense of continuity with history. Instead, its connection to heritage has become an inherently intangible one, carried through personal stories, memory and community narratives as much as through buildings themselves. This human-centred approach appears to have infused the way Rotterdam engages with culture and heritage more broadly. Combined with its identity as a port city with a long history of migration and cultural diversity, it creates a distinctive context, one that sets Rotterdam apart from cities that can rely on an imposing stock of built heritage as a source of attractiveness and local pride.

title: Hub releases second “In Varietate Concordia” Podcast episode featuring Sabine Verheyen
content:
Following the inaugural episode with Portuguese pianist Maria João Pires, the In Varietate Concordia Podcast presents a conversation between Sabine Verheyen, First Vice-President of the European Parliament, and Sneška Quaedvlieg-Mihailović,  Secretary General of Europa Nostra and Project Leader of the European Heritage Hub. They discuss the political and economic value of culture, the history and layers of the European identity, and what Europe needs to do for the cultural sector. 

Together, they “travel” to the city of Aachen, where Ms. Verheyen spent her childhood and began her political career, and trace the threads that led her to become one of the most fervent advocates for culture and cultural heritage in the European political landscape.

title: Join the Hub’s deep-dive webinar on inclusive heritage case studies from Rotterdam, Umbria and Antwerp
content:
On 18 September, join the European Heritage Hub for the webinar “Sharing Local Stories: Cultural Heritage for Inclusive Cities and Regions”. 

During this session, we will dive into the key lessons from our recent Peer-Learning Visit to Rotterdam from 18-20 June, and discover connected initiatives in other European cities and regions! You will get insights into the content of the visit, including recommendations for cities, regions and cultural heritage stakeholders, from the expert who facilitated the Peer-Learning programme. You will also learn about two case studies from the participating cultural heritage practitioners.

  • Tanja Mlaker, Director Cultuur Eindhoven (The Netherlands) – Hub Peer-Learning Visit expert
  • Martijn van der Mark, City of Rotterdam (The Netherlands) – Hub Peer-Learning Visit host
  • Greet Donckers, Cultural Heritage Consultant, City of Antwerp (Belgium)
  • Gianluigi Bettin, Project Manager, Sviluppumbria – Regional agency of economic development in Umbria (Italy)
snippet: On 18 September, join the European Heritage Hub for the webinar “Sharing Local Stories: Cultural Heritage for Inclusive Cities and Regions”.

title: The State of Democracy Depends on Who Can Sit Next to You in the Cinema
content:
During the European Digital Cinema Forum Conference of 2026 in Warsaw, Poland, Natalia Baydan, a manager of the Planeta Kino cinema operating in Kyiv, spoke about the situation of the cinema sector during Russia’s war against Ukraine. Roman Romanchuk, manager of a Ukrainian cinema chain, also participated in the conversation on-site in Warsaw. From the discussion, we learned about how rising energy prices affect cinema operations, as well as about the staff shortages caused by the fact that young men — who previously made up the majority of people employed as projectionists — are now serving on the frontlines.

What stayed with me the most, however, were the stories about what cinema, as a cultural phenomenon, can become for people affected by crisis — in this case, by war. Despite the fact that screenings are often interrupted by the sound of sirens, Ukrainians continue to go to the cinema. This is because people in the midst of a crisis still want to come together and share stories on screen together; because it is almost like a holiday which, in the current situation, people cannot otherwise have; and finally, because it represents two hours of normalcy in an abnormal world.

title: Bridging the Heritage-Investment Gap
content:
How is heritage in Europe financed? Independent local heritage organisations typically rely on a mix of public funds and philanthropy. This funding model has enabled them to grow and to have an impact on their cities and beyond — yet it has its limitations. I propose it is time to rethink our approach to fundraising and to explore new frameworks of capturing the value heritage creates, including impact investment.

The work of heritage organisations aims to benefit the public. Over the last seven years, thanks to the efforts of The Collective Foundation, of which I am a core member, the rivers in the city of Sofia run cleaner and are prioritised in urban policy. The value created in terms of a healthier and more pleasant urban environment, captured carbon, biodiversity, and city branding, is hard to measure. But maybe heritage activists like us should be trying harder to do so. We could be going much further in measuring impact and — here is a bold idea — capturing some of the value we generate in terms of monetary returns. We could then reinvest those funds in activating further heritage sites. What a win for heritage that would be.
